utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Lisa Biersay on behalf of the Prosecution, along with STA Douglas Stringer, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, and our legal intern, Moritz von Normann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, along with Ruzica Ciric and Michael Connelly, legal interns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the legal advisor for Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Terzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Seselj. May I remind that you are still under oath. Ms. Biersay, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would you allow me three minutes, only three minutes, to address the Trial Chamber. I believe it would be very important for me to do that. Three minutes only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I apologise. The Trial Chamber didn't invite me to make comment, but at this time the Prosecution would oppose Mr. Seselj giving a three-minute speech essentially not knowing what is he going say and given his inclination of what we consider to be inflammatory language and speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why the Prosecution opposes to this request of Mr. Seselj not knowing what he would say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't intend to use any inflammatory words. I just want to address the Trial Chamber and talk to them for three minutes to provide them with a piece of information. That's all. I believe that you will be interested in what I have to say to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, is that a piece of information with regard to this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with regard to this case, and the importance of the information is huge. And it will not be inflammatory because you can't say anything inflammatory in three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is not -- for me, the question is not whether it is inflammatory or not. The question is this -- these proceedings are party-driven. The parties decide on what they want to put forward in court. Mr. Zivanovic decided upon what he would like to ask you and what he did not ask you, so it is not your decision to add information that perhaps Mr. Zivanovic doesn't want you to elicit it -- elicit. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this has nothing to do with the examination-in-chief that was led yesterday by Mr. Zivanovic. I would like to remind you of the proceedings from other cases. In my case, for example, one witness wanted to greet me and we kissed each other in the middle of the courtroom. There are a lot of such proceedings showing that the Trial Chamber allowed the accused to address them. I'm only asking for three minutes. The three minutes are already over. I would have already finished if the -- if Ms. Biersay did not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have three minutes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday Ms. Biersay claimed that I never put my accusations against Vesna Bosanac face to face. I looked at the transcript from my case yesterday evening, and I realised that at the end of Vesna Bosanac's testimony I asked the floor and then I lay great charges at her expense. Judge Antonetti interrupted me and ordered that everything I had said should be removed from the transcript. That's why my words are not in the transcript and his order is. And then he apologised to Vesna Bosanac and then he gave us a break. I'm finishing. After the break, which was a normal break, we had a discussion or a debate for over half an hour involving Judge Antonetti, Prosecutor Mundis, and myself about the principle of using Rule -- and applying Rule 92 ter in the case. I was right, your professional services may check that, and you can have that on your screens within a minute. I did speak, I did say, I did confront Vesna Bosanac but Judge Antonetti ordered my words to be erased from the transcript. I have finished and thank you very much. And it was even less than three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You want to intervene at this point in time, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think the time has passed, Your Honour, but thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Seselj. I'd like to talk to you about your evidence about the 200 executed at Ovcara. Do you remember that from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If -- I'd like to repeat what I understand you to be saying. If I understand you correctly, you are saying that those 200 remained in the custody of the JNA and that they were never turned over to the civilian authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not -- there's not a single piece of evidence that they were turned over. Ms. Biersay, you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You answered my question. You said yes. And now I'd like -- I'll give you an opportunity, but first, I need to set the foundational questions first. So I understood that correctly. Thank you. Now, if I also understand your Milosevic testimony, there it was your testimony that the 200 executed were turned over to the civilian authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I thought at the time. I didn't lie. That was my mindset at the time, based on what I had read in the media up to then, and based on the outcome of the proceedings conducted before the supreme court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe General Gojovic was the president of the supreme military court in Belgrade at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I see. If we could now turn to Defence tab 19, I believe it is, which is 1D02805. And I'm interested in beginning at page 61.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gojovic. I said it. It wasn't recorded. [In English] "I believe General Gojovic was the president of the supreme ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honours. The same document I tried yesterday to show to the witness and the Prosecution objected, and I object on the same ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I am showing his previous inconsistent statement which is perfectly admissible, I would think, in -- during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Zivanovic. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is -- it was quite legitimate for me to show the witness and explore this issue with him during my examination-in-chief, and I don't believe that different -- different standards should be applied to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. My memory, if it serves me properly, is that my objection was based on the manner in which Mr. Zivanovic was trying to use this, and it was an issue of memory, if the Trial Chamber recalls, because the Trial Chamber did deliberate on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the Prosecution opposed to the -- to the use of this document to -- and to explore with the witness something that was in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Zivanovic, for the reason Ms. Biersay mentioned, and now is there different reason. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So I know that before you -- it sounds like your English is quite good and the transcript before you is in English, and I will read it in English and they'll translate it for you just so I can put it on the record. So this --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand a word of English. I can only speak English. I cannot listen to the English language. Everything has to be translated into Serbian for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Understood. Let me begin at page 43604 of this transcript, which is your testimony in the Milosevic case on 1 September 2005. And you were asked a question about the events relating to Ovcara. And this was your answer: "A. I know something about these events because I made efforts to find out, but I'm not an eye-witness. And what I found out is rather reliable; namely that the authorities of the Autonomous District of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem asked the JNA that some prisoners from the Vukovar Hospital be turned over to them, with a demand that they be tried for the crimes that they had previously committed over the civilian population of Vukovar. And the information I got is that a certain number - I don't know exactly how many - of those prisoners were turned over to them, after which the prisoners were taken to the farm called Ovcara whereupon the execution of those prisoners occurred. "Q. From all that you managed to find out, who was involved? Was the JNA involved in any way?"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this. I have not finished reading. And I don't know what Mr. Seselj is pulling out of his briefcase and we would strongly object to this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you -- indeed, you should wait for the questions to put to you. And may we ask what you are pulling out of your briefcase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sincerely thought that Ms. Biersay had finished reading, and I started answering her question. And as for my briefcase, this is a previous statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There was -- Mr. Seselj, there was no question at all. She was still reading, and even if she finished reading, there was no question yet. And say again, please, what is it you took out of your briefcase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I've pulled out are two folders. In one of them, there is a statement that I gave Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Hadzic's legal representative. And in the other, there are several documents, including copies of my book, "The Defence Witness for Slobodan Milosevic in The Hague." I published my entire testimony and I photocopied those parts which Ms. Biersay is partly quoting from. She's not quoting the entire thing. She has chosen only some parts to quote from. If you want me to take -- put them back into my briefcase, I can do that. I can also offer to make photocopies for you, because I myself published that book and it was published in 21.000 copies. It was published in English. It's available on the Internet. I can provide you with all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We would appreciate, Mr. Seselj, if you would put the documents back in your briefcase as you offered to do. The parties, of course, know all of this, and I repeat once again, that the -- the proceedings are in the hands of the parties. They decide on what they want to show to Court, what they want to ask you, and what they want to hear from you as the truth as you know it. Please continue, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "Q. From all that you managed to find out, who was involved? Was the JNA involved in any way? "A. According to my information, not a single officer of the JNA was involved. And from what I learned, it was some locals who did it, who had some outstanding accounts with the prisoners, but I have no direct knowledge about" --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is -- if we could continue. I've stopped reading. If we can continue to the next page, which is page 61 in e-court. "... but I have no direct knowledge about it because I wasn't there."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You also continued, Mr. Seselj, to say: "I dealt with it because it was one of the charges in my indictment, so I had to research it extensively and my experts are working on it, and the knowledge I have was obtained actually by my expert." Now, you go on to talk about Aleksandar Vasiljevic, and Judge Kwon asked you about this first-hand information that you said you had: "What do you mean by first-hand, Mr. Seselj?" And you replied: "I learned from people who were there. There is reliable information that I got because I dealt with this question, in a way." And Judge Kwon asked you: "From whom did you hear that?" And you answered: "I talked to a large number of people. I talked, in particular, to the commander of the Leva Supoderica Unit, Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni. I couldn't even tell you the names of all the people with whom I discussed it." That's what you said in the Milosevic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I demand that I may be allowed to answer as extensively as the question was. You did not put it on paper so it is not easy for me remember everything you said. You want me to start answering immediately?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My question to you is simply: By hearing the interpretation that you had, is that what you said during the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have made here a compilation of my statements made during that testimony. You cherry-picked what you believe necessary to put forward now but you left certain things out. For instance, I see that one sentence is missing here, that my investigators are still working on it. Why did you omit that? It is in my statement. It is also in the transcript. I mean in the recording of my testimony. Now, my knowledge up to that moment was as follows. I mentioned yesterday Milan Lancuzanin known as Kameni. I insisted on finding out from him whether the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party had been involved. He said no. I also had consistent information from the media that all the prisoners had been handed over. And, third, there was the investigation, the inquiry, carried out in Belgrade and such was the outcome. I studied it the first years I've --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- spent in The Hague but at that time I did not have legal advisors and no privileged communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment, please. I understand this because you explained it extensively to Mr. Zivanovic, and I -- you answered my question that this, in fact, is information that you gave the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case. I understand your position about that. My question to you is: Do I understand you correctly that you're saying that your information is more accurate now than it was in 2005, when you testified? Yes or no, your information is more accurate now?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I have incomparably more accurate information, but I'm not ever going to answer you with a yes or no because this is not a TV quiz. I am testifying here with full awareness of the importance of my evidence, and you cannot manipulate me as you do other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. So, Mr. Seselj, is it fair to say that you tailor the facts to exonerate yourself or certain accused charged before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never tailored any fact in favour of my own Defence or the Defence of Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Karadzic, or Mr. Hadzic. I found out here in The Hague and Sljivancanin confessed in his own case that he had brought the buses with prisoners to Ovcara; whereas I had earlier thought that the prisoners had been handed over to the civilian authorities in the Vukovar barracks. Here you called many witnesses in my trial and you provided me with their statements, statements of victims, survivors from Ovcara, Emil Cakalic and others, from which it is evident that the JNA officers were at Ovcara all the time. They compared lists. They released them, et cetera. So you subsequently showered me with information here that runs counter to what I had thought. Now the first witness in my trial, Goran Stoparic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj -- Mr. Seselj, one moment, please --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... recounted here how he had made arrangements with Kameni --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment, please. I think you have answered my question loud and clearly. And --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may think so, but I didn't. I have one more sentence. Please, do not run away from the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One more sentence, okay.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] One more sentence. [Interpretation] Goran Stoparic stated here that he, Kameni, and Kinez got together on somebody's instructions or somebody's demand over there, I can't remember who, to agree how they should testify, give the same evidence to exonerate Sljivancanin. Before I heard him --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I had completely different information. I was taken aback. I was surprised. You're again running away from the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to, if we could -- I believe this is tab 100, which is 65 ter 4955.1. And this is a video-clip. And pursuant to our internal protocol, I wanted to check with the interpreters to see if they have been able to locate the transcript for this video, 4955.1, which, for the record, is an extract from the main exhibit, from 30 minute, 08, to 31 minute, 11, and I believe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So before we start playing, Mr. Seselj, I'd like you just to take a look at this video. And then after it's finished, I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "These are our volunteers who are part of the Territorial Defence. We haven't got any units of our own here. All the people are our people. All the units here are our units. And, of course, those who came here of their own will to fight, know full well why they are here and what they're fighting for, and they don't need to be persuaded to fight because they themselves wanted to do so. And therefore one should not be surprised at their courage. "Q. How significant is the liberation of Vukovar for Serbia and the Serbian people? "Vojislav Seselj: It is of exceptional significance, exceptional significance. This is the most powerful Ustasha stronghold. Once Vukovar is taken, Ustashas have no chance of saving either Osijek or Vinkovci. There is nothing to stop our forces. Vukovar is the key line that needs to be broken through, that needs to be captured, and then there will be nothing Ustashas can do. The Ustashas know that if Vukovar falls here, if Slunj falls in Serbian Krajina, then Tudjman's Ustashas regime in Zagreb will fall too. And that is why this battle is decisive."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You recognised yourself, of course, I take it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, I'm impressed at how good I looked and how well I spoke at that time, and I hope that you are impressed too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But, of course. Now, Mr. Seselj, do you recall the occasion on which you gave this interview? According to our information, it was not long before the liberation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have been after 8 November. It could have been during my first visit in October, or during my second visit, on the 8th of November. It couldn't have been later. And Vukovar was liberated on 18 November; that is to say, ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it's accurate at the time, was it not, that the volunteers, "our volunteers," your volunteers, made up a part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Territorial Defence was part of the Motorised Guards Brigade, completely integrated into their complement. And the 1st Assault Detachment, which participated the most in the fighting for Vukovar, was made up, if I remember well, of three companies of the Guards Brigade, two companies of the Territorial Defence, and the detachment called Leva Supoderica. That was the composition of the assault detachment commanded by Major Borivoje Trajkovic. This is exhaustive information, and this is something that I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 4955.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3556, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to a document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. 3256. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: A document which has already been admitted as P2625, and it's tab 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you can see it already on your screen, Mr. Seselj, and --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you make it a bit larger? I don't see very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that better?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I recognise the document, but I can't read it very well yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Slobodan Katic, his name appears at the very bottom. You know who that is; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Katic was the commander of a group of volunteers that had arrived with him from Belgrade and was integrated into the Leva Supoderica Unit. Because of his merits in the war, I later proclaimed him a Chetnik vojvoda, duke, too. However, when Vukovar was liberated, he stayed to live in Vukovar and he got married there. And I believe he continued to live there until the Croats recaptured Vukovar again in the beginning of early 1996, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now this document is dated 9 December 1991, and it's a request for promotion for the people listed below; right? So you have Katic and he's proposing -- he's asking the chief of the War Staff, Ljubisa Petkovic and his deputy Zoran Rankic from Belgrade to propose the following warriors for promotion, right? That's what's happening in this document?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, this document did not exist at the War Staff. It was never registered in the protocol. It was the private property of Ljubisa Petkovic and he turned it over to the OTP, to the investigators. Indeed, Slobodan Katic did address Ljubisa Petkovic and his deputy asking for the promotion of all these people but they are not members of the Serbian Radical Party, and I cannot understand what kinds of sentiment this reflects, whether Ljubisa Petkovic was supposed to influence somehow his connections in the War Staff or what. None of them was in the Leva Supoderica Unit, except for Milan Lancuzanin, known as Kameni, and Kameni was in the first group that I proclaimed Chetnik vojvodas. I don't know any of the other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, this is not a request to the JNA for promotion to these people; right? This request is going to the chief of the SRS War Staff and Zoran Rankic, not to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, ignorant, unschooled people are incapable of using the proper form when they write something. Slobodan Katic did not have much schooling. He was a good warrior but not very educated. We did not have any agreement with the JNA, and the first officer ranks were granted by Duke Momcilo Djujic on the 13th of May, 1991, at Ravna Gora, and he promoted into officers all members of our volunteer group that had fought in Borovo Selo. There are more cases -- was I now cut off? There are more cases. It's important for me to tell you this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Seselj. We'll get there. But what I wanted to do now is to show you another document, which is tab 35, P2576. And while we're waiting for it to be brought to the screen, it is dated 9 November 1991. And the signature at the bottom is -- it's written that this is Ljubisa Petkovic signing this document. And it's addressed to the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment. And in the first paragraph it notes that: "All the volunteers that the Serbian Radical Party has sent you are being placed under your command and the protection of the Vukovar TO. The SRS War Staff has appointed Slobodan Katic, a brave and experienced soldier from Belgrade, as the commander or the komandant of the volunteers in Vukovar." Is that consistent with the information that you have?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not clear enough. Slobodan Katic was appointed by the War Staff as commander of the group that had arrived with him on the 9th of November. Ljubisa Petkovic knows about the order of the commander of the Guards Brigade to send volunteers to the unit. This group of volunteers was taken to Bubanj Potok. They got weapons there and uniforms, and they were bussed to Vukovar. This is a letter that he was sending with Slobodan Katic. I don't see anything odd about it. It's not perfectly articulate or literate, but I don't see anything problematic about the content.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if I could just check with the interpreters before we get there, it would be 88 -- P88.50.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We've got it. In fact, we have two of them: 50.3 and 50.8.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And could I also confirm that the interpreters have P1740?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, some of your very early contacts with people in Borovo Selo was with Vukasin Soskocanin. Excuse me for my pronunciation. Do you recall that person, Soskocanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Vukasin Soskocanin very well. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Borovo Selo. And the last time I saw him was in April 1991, when we agreed about the integration of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in your -- you recall giving an interview for the documentary "Death of Yugoslavia" to Laura Silber?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave that interview. It was more than 30 minutes and they actually used only five minutes. But I published the entire interview in one of my books. I could not allow all the smart things I said to go unheard.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe in that interview that he provided your volunteers with weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukasin Soskocanin? Yes. Our volunteers went there wearing civilian clothes and no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you explained that later on you developed contacts with the Serbian police and also with the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, those were our contacts, of course, but all these contacts were done through Ljubisa Petkovic. I was never in the security service or the Serbian police in general or the General Staff of the JNA. And I never personally visited the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ. But we did have these contacts on a number of issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Sure. So you would have people who worked for you deal with contacts with other people. You didn't do everything yourself. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. You see, Ljubisa Petkovic went as one of my men both to the State Security Service and the General Staff, and then, in the meantime, the State Security Service recruited him to work for them against the party. And when I heard about that, I interrogated Ljubisa Petkovic before TV cameras and after that he was expelled from the party. And he confirmed all that. He even confirmed that the State Security Service had given him a car for his use, and he took out a driving licence on which was written "the MUP of Serbia," the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: He was expelled from the party. But you had a reconciliation during the course of your trial; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Petkovic was questioned by OTP investigators several times. He provided very extensive statements. He provided documents that he had in his possession, that is to say, documents he had had at home, and he collaborated with the OTP all the way up until the Security Council decided that no new indictments could be raised. In fact they decided that all the indictments had to be issued by the beginning of 2005. Ljubisa Petkovic was scared because he was threatened with an indictment. He was very co-operative with investigators until that time and he even brought them new witnesses for interview. However, when he realised that there could be no indictment against him any longer, he addressed my assistants. He offered his co-operation and assistance, and he gave them even a copy of a long interview he had given to OTP investigators, and that was in 2006 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that is pure truth. And, of course, we embraced him because he was useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: He was useful. And in fact, Mr. Petkovic refused to testify in your trial as either a witness for the Prosecution or a witness for the Trial Chamber, and he was convicted of contempt for that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the reason why after a while we appointed him a Member of Parliament. One MP happened to die after the elections. That was Dragan Tasic, a legal assistant of mine. He was a graduate of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- university in Montpellier. He spoke perfect French, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he died, we rewarded Ljubisa Petkovic by offering him his seat in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's been brought to my attention that I think at transcript page 15 what's written is "Borivoje Trajkovic" in relation to the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment. Do you recall the commander?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Many newspapers published our photograph during our inspection of the front line in Vukovar, and I even said that, on one occasion, Borivoje Trajkovic complained that he had had a lot of trouble because of that photograph because when we made an alliance with Milosevic, he got into trouble over that --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he later became commander of the gendarme service and a general. I want to provide you with complete information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is the name Borivoje Tesic familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it's my mistake. It's not Borivoje Trajkovic. It's Borivoje Tesic. He was the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment. It was my slip of the tongue. He posed for a photograph together with me at that time, and it was published in all the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke because there was also a man called Borivoje Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj -- I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If the interpreters could now go to the P1740. May I just have a confirmation. I know you said it before, I just -- directing my comments to the interpreters. I just want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time I'd like to play P1740, which is also tab 129.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Dr. Vojislav Seselj, president of the Serbian Radical Party, visited Borovo Selo today. "Seselj: The Serbian people located in the most endangered areas have to persevere. They have to show as much patience and will as possible as they are bearing a heavy burden. Most things depend on their strength, courage, and determination. "Reporter: Are the units of your party ready to help at this moment? "Seselj: We have no party units. What we do is organising the registration of volunteers in Serbia and then sending them where they are needed; i.e., they are going to the villages where they are asked to come by Serbian villagers and they're immediately joining the local units under the command of the village staff. That means that we do not have any special units in this region nor do we have the need for them. We are all Serbs regardless of the party affiliation. We are not taking into account the party divisions until the borders of Serbia are secured. "Reporter: Vojislav Seselj, president of the Serbian Radical Party, met with the Orthodox bishop Lukijan from the ... Osijek-Polje, who, among other things, said the following: All Serbs must be unanimous as that is in their best interest. Enough with the divisions."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And so, Mr. Seselj, this is an accurate reflection of what was happening at the time. Namely that your volunteers were being asked to go to certain villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday and I'm confirming it today. Yes, this clip was taken in Borovo Selo in April. I suppose. First we sent them to Borovo Selo and then we started selling [as interpreted] them to other endangered villages. I can give you some of the names of those villages, if you wish, if you are interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, please, tell us just the names of the villages that you remember.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trpinja, Tenja, Mirkovci, Laslovo, and Ernestinovo. Tomislav Nikolic, the current president of the Republic of Serbia, also fought there, and as a result, he was also bestowed the title of a Chetnik vojvoda. There are other villages that I can try and remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Regarding your comment about Mirkovci, if I could now please turn to tab 150, and this is P1741. I think this relates to what you're describing.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Some patience, please. And this appears to be coming from the Mirkovci local community going to the Serbian Radical Party in Belgrade. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was signed by Zoran Beldar who was the president of the local commune of Mirkovci. He thanked us for our assistance consisting of our volunteers who were sent there. He emphasises three persons who played an especially prominent role - Kosta Carina, Nenad Vukanovic, Ranislav Dragojlovic. I can tell that you that Kosta Carina was their leader, and I can tell you that they captured the state-of-the-art Armbrust rocket-launcher which is used in antitank struggle. They brought it to my office in Belgrade. We held a press conference and we demonstrated that piece of weaponry and that was aired on all Serbian television channels. Maybe Ljubisa Petkovic could have provided with you that clip because he was the one who kept them. I fully confirm this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One clarification, Mr. Seselj, because the last name is not yet entered on the transcript. For Zoran. You said: "The president of the local community was Zoran," could you spell the last name, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beldar. That's his -- [In English] Beldar, B-e-l-d-a-r. [Interpretation] You see how good I am spelling, Ms. Biersay? I don't speak English at all, but I can spell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Quite remarkable. Mr. Seselj, could you describe for us your view about whether or not Baranja is, in fact, Croatian territory historically.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baranja was never Croatian territory, absolutely never. It was part of Hungary. It did not belong to any of the counties which subsequently became parts of Croatia. It never belonged to the county of Slavonia, for example. After the First World War, a great national council of Serbs and people from Bunjevo [phoen] called Bunjevci -- Bunjevci are a Slav people very close to us Serbs. They met -- Bunjevci have their idiosyncrasies in their culture and language and they reached a decision that Banat, Backa, and Baranja would directly join Serbia. After the Second World War, however, the Communists made Baranja a Croatian territorial unit. Croats will have to return Baranja and all the other Serbian lands to us, sooner or later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So am I correct that in your view, Baranja properly belongs to the territories that belong to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you describe the famous line that is the western border of what would be Serbian lands, the one that runs through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the line Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica. And that line actually is why I should go down in history.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to a document and -- tab 118, previously admitted exhibit 2955.2913. This is a newspaper article, and it doesn't ...

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't see it yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. It's coming. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this has to be enlarged. I think that only the text you are interested in should be on the screen. It would automatically be larger, and I would be able to read it then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I am interested in the article called: "Western borders of Slavonia now open."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see, this is Goran Hadzic's press conference, but I cannot read the text. If you want my comments on the text, you will have to provide me with a hard copy of the article. The letters are too small for my age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just let you know we have it in hard copy in original size and we could provide it to the witness, but not right now from -- approximately for several minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll move on in a different way. In the same document could we scroll into the English -- to the English translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I am -- perhaps can you see. It's the section that says: "Ilija Petrovic." If you can't see it, I'll read it to you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, it says "Ilija Petrovic" who is identified as the information minister. You knew him; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember him. Yesterday I mentioned Ilija Petkovic and Ilija Koncarevic. Ilija Petrovic, that doesn't ring a bell. I don't know that I ever met him. His deputy was Rade Leskovac. He was well connected on Serbian TV. That's why he was very often seen giving statements instead of the minister himself. I may have met him but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to read you -- into the record what this says. It says: "The information minister in Hadzic's government recalled that the proposal of the Serbian National Council of these districts was to establish the contentious western border along Ilova-Virovitica stretch if necessary by moving the Serbian and Croatian population [sic]." And my question to you: The Ilova-Virovitica line would be the very northern-most boundaries of the line that you mentioned earlier, the one for which you should go down in history?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This line is much more modest than mine. Less challenging or demanding, if you will. My line comprises a lot more, significantly a lot more territory. That's why I will go down in history and not Ilija Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your line, of course, also cuts down over in the Knin Krajina area; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, with regard to Slavonia itself, my line encompasses much more territory than the one starting in Ilova. If you look at the line Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac and then onwards to Virovitica, you will see that that comprises a lot more territory than the Ilova-Virovitica line. If you had a map, I could show it to you on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you about is the idea of population exchanges. You have previously said that you advocated population exchanges in certain situations; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, you charged only me with that. Although many people advocated that. In Croatia it started with Tudjman. Dobrica Cosic adopted that idea. There was a meeting somewhere on the Adriatic coast, I don't know where exactly. He actually met up with Tudjman in order to agree that. It was to be a civilised exchange of population where differences could not be reconciled. It was a repeating theme. I was not the only one. Ilija Petrovic was not the only one who mentioned it. Many, many politicians - more of them on the Croatian side than on the Serbian side - kept on mentioning that. The Croats were the ones who started mass expulsion of the Serbs in 1990 already, and later on they decided to put forth that proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- just to clarify, is -- or was this question still based on the document we have in front of us at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Not regarding Mr. Seselj's own views about the population exchange, and it was based on the attribution to Petrovic about moving the Serbian and Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My concern was the word "exchange" and "exchanging," because in this document, it said "moving."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Exactly. So my question to Mr. Seselj was about his view of population exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But not about population moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: There's no question yet, Mr. Seselj. If you could wait for one minute while I show you another document, which I believe is tab 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, the document -- the hard copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We provided the document [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The hard is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's okay. I've finished. I don't need it anymore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You've finished the document. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I did not fully answer your question. I did not give you a full answer. It says: "Moving the Croatian and Serbian populations." This is an exchange. If it was only Croatian or only Serbian, it would be a different thing. However, if the populations of two ethnic groups move at the same time, this constitutes an exchange. It is not done subsequently. It is done at the same time, one move to the place from which the others have moved out. That's an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So I take it that you agree with what Ilija Petrovic is saying in this article.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in what way do you disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with him at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in what way do you disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree in terms of the western border of the Serbian Slavonia or in terms of people moving out. It was only in 1992 that I started advocating the idea of the exchange of population when 300.000 Serbian refugees and displaced persons arrived in Serbia. In 1991, I believe that I was never in favour of this idea, unless you have something to prove that I did. It was only when Serbia was swamped with refugees from Croatia that I started advocating the idea of the exchange of population as a partial solution to the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now have tab 60, which is 65 ter 155.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Seselj, this is a transcript of an interview given on 24 May 1991 with you called: "Chetnik revenge will be blind." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it, and yes, the revenge will be blind. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could go to -- actually, Mr. Seselj, we'll come back to this document.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So should I retain it in my memory until then?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, no need.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll move to another 65 ter number, which is 65 ter number 6613. And for the Trial Chamber, that is tab 138. If we could go to the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So I am interested in the portion that begins: "However regarding Croatia," and I think it begins at the bottom of the page that you're looking at in Serbian. Do you see it? It says: "However, regarding Croatia, we, the Serbian Chetniks, are constantly telling to the new Ustasha leader Franjo Tudjman ..." Do you see that, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, can this be enlarged just a little? Can you highlight only that part and put it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that any better?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't you read it and I will listen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you can't see it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: With difficulty. You read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You say here: "The new Ustasha leader, Franjo Tudjman, and the new Ustasha authorities in Croatia not to play games with the Serbian people that lives in the areas of the present improvised Croatian state community. This is the Serbian territory, populated by the Serbian people, and we shall never allow it to be separated from its mother country. The Croats may separate themselves from Yugoslavia; in other words, they may have an independent state, may merge with someone else. However, they must know at all times that at all costs that the price of new rivers of blood, we shall not let them separate any territory that contains Serbian villages, Serbian mass graves, Serbian slaughter-houses, Serbian pits, Serbian camps, Serbian Jasenovac, destroyed Serbian churches. We shall never allow that."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should now show the last page of the interview. We need to see the date. Or perhaps you can just give us the date. Please take a look and give us the date. And then I'll just pretend that I believe you. There should be the date on the last page and the place where this was published or the name of the journalist, or perhaps it was a TV show. I'm sure that it was a TV show but -- because it says "presenter." Do you have the entire interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We do but not in our electric electronic system and I can get that after the break. But my question to is now is: Based on what I've just read, it sounds like what you're saying here, it's that wherever Serb villages, Serb mass graves, slaughter-houses, pits, camps, churches were, that that was Serbian -- Serb territory. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you did not fully understand me because you're absolutely not familiar with those things. I am saying that the results of genocide should not be recognised, and I'm talking about the genocide that Croatians committed against the Serbian people during the Second World War. The Croats wanted to erase what happened during the Second World War and then to establish borders according to the current ethnic composition. Our position was we should not admit that the number of the Serbian population was -- has been reduced because they were killed during the Second World War. The Croats cannot enjoy the fruit of the genocide that they had committed against the Serbian people. I said this sometime in the first half of 1991, before the war started, if my memory serves me properly. That's why you are not very keen on giving us the date and the place. However, if you are a serious Prosecutor, you should always have that information at the tip of your fingers. You have to have that information. You should have preceded this question by giving us the time and the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I would do if I were in your shoes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you confirm that this, in fact, is in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm this because this could have been in 1990. However, judging from the contents you can tell that the war had -- did not start yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I see the time for the break, Your Honours. I'm happy to stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Biersay. We take the first break, 30 minutes. We will be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you recall attending the Great National Assembly of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could have tab 4, please, which is P22.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I'm sure it will need to be expanded for you, Mr. Seselj. It's the article discussing "constitutional law adopted." And you can see at the top, it says: "Meeting of the Great National Assembly of the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Beli Manastir, 25 September." Now, what I'm interested in is actually found on page 3 in the English and it should be towards the end of the -- this article, and I believe the paragraph begins: "Seselj went on to say ..." Actually it's the paragraph that begins: "'Your Territorial Defence has restored the glory of Serbian soldiers,'" said Dr. Vojislav Seselj, addressing the deputies." Do you see that in the Serbian?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not before me. Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Does this refresh your recollection about whether or not you attended that session, that assembly --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why did you go to that meeting; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somebody must have invited me or informed me, and I went there to give my support to the highest body of the legislative branch of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I gave my support through my presence and my speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I take it at this time you had no political conflict with Goran Hadzic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I really didn't even know Goran Hadzic at that time. He was at this session, and maybe we shook hands in passing, but I don't remember that we ever talked. We could have met. We could have shaken hands, but that's all. I knew much better Caslav Ocic, for instance, who was also elected foreign minister. And I also -- I already told you about Ilija Koncarevic and Mr. Petkovic. One of them must have invited me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different topic regarding Arkan. You described yesterday in great detail your conflict with him when he threatened you; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I returned the threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I take it you also knew that, by reputation, he was wanted by Interpol?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I wasn't really informed about that. There was talk that he had robbed banks in Sweden. There were stories of that kind. But in 1986, I was interested in him as a means to target Stane Dolanc. Arkan was then an unimportant person, whereas Stane Dolanc was one of the top leaders in Yugoslavia and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. So you're saying that all the information that you had about him being a bank robber and all those -- all that criminal activity, that was information you had in the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had information that he was involved in the murder of Djurekovic. And yesterday when I returned to Scheveningen, I saw on TV that Germany had asked the Serbian authorities to issue a certificate confirming that Arkan is dead or that he is alive, what a coincidence. Obviously the Germans have the same information and you had much better contact with Arkan. He negotiated with you in order to be relieved from prosecution to appear as a witness in exchange in the Milosevic and some other trials.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean you personally. I mean the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You and Arkan had this personal conflict but you reconciled in 1991 at the funeral of a volunteer; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was real reconciliation. We shook hands then. Perhaps we exchanged a couple of words. That's when Mirko Lovadinovic, known as Uco, got killed. He was a volunteer in Slavonia. And when a group of our volunteers withdrew, he had decided to stay and join Arkan and his men, and he got killed fighting with Arkan's Men. And Arkan and I both attended his funeral. And a similar thing happened to another person. I think it happened twice. There was another meeting I had with Arkan when Arkan came to my home. Are you interested in that? In November --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In November --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you interested?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In November of what year?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in October, 31st October 1992. I can tell you all about it if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, let me show you these documents first and perhaps we'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like now to have tab 145, which is P1743. It's been previously admitted. And this interview, the date of it, is given as 29 November 1991. The B/C/S page, I think it's -- it begins at the very end of the third page. I think it should say page 123 at the bottom of the B/C/S text. And so the very bottom, which hopefully we can enlarge for Mr. Seselj. And, in the English in which I'm interested, at -- is on page 2. Before we move to the Arkan part that I want to -- to go to, I just wanted to address an issue on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, so the part I'm interested in is the part that starts: "The army has already cleansed its ranks ..." Do you see that text? I'm sure you're familiar with it as it's your -- you published it. So it says on page --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "The army has already cleansed its ranks quite a bit. It should keep cleansing them and cleanse them to the maximum ..." Further on it says: "Now we trust the army, because the army has shown -- show us in practice that it is fighting to defend the Serbian people, Serbian territories, our western borders. The army is acting in co-operation with all of our men, and without their acting in co-operation, neither one of them would have achieved the results which are being achieved." And that is the view that you held at the time that you gave this interview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now going to page 7 in the English, and I believe it's the very end of 124 in B/C/S. It's a sentence that carries over into 125. Okay. I believe we have the B/C/S well situated. And for the English we need to go back a few pages to get to the portion that I want.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which excerpt have you shown me in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It will be the very -- the very last -- "sto," the very last thing that you see, "sto" on the last line on that page. You see where there is a period and then it begins "sto ..."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that but I need the -- the continuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As for ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could go in the English go -- go backwards one more page. Okay. There we go. And if, for the English, if you could enlarge the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, if you could -- you've read that -- that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could now move in the B/C/S to the next page, 125, at the very top.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a question about co-operation, and here it says: "As far as the Serbian Volunteers Guard, headed by Zeljko, Arkan, Raznjatovic, is concerned, we co-operate with them and our men have participated in many battles together." Does that correctly reflect the situation when you gave this interview in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One point should be cleared up here. The statement is correct, it was correctly quoted. It was the end of November 1991. In the course of that month of November, our volunteers, just as Arkan's volunteers, were under command of Radovan Stojicic, known as Badza, in the Operative Group North commanded by the Novi Sad Corps. So Arkan's Men were there as well. They took part in some combat such as the battle for Tenja, but the two groups of fighters did not mix. Both of them were engaged but they did not join together and they did not mix. We were under the same command but each had their own section of the front line where they fought. And my aim at that time was not to increase tensions between me and Arkan so that our people, our men on the ground, would not clash mutually. That was my concern. Because on a couple of occasions, a conflict, an armed conflict, a skirmish between our two groups of men was barely avoided.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to tab 151, which is 65 ter 2039.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If you just be patient while we find this document.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have all the time in the world for you, Ms. Biersay. I like you best of all the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in -- in the B/C/S, I think we can go forward to page 10 to 11 in the B/C/S, and I think it also corresponds to pages 10 to 11 in the English as well. And this is an extract of an interview given to B92 and it was republished in April of 1994. So 65 ter 2039.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My colleague made it even easier than I thought. So only the two pages of the B/C/S are in -- are uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this, Mr. Seselj, if I can ask you what information at the time did you have about Arkan and the criminal activities that he was involved with in Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information about his robberies and looting. I knew about several murders he committed. I once even filed a criminal complaint about the murder of Iso Lero. Arkan's Men kidnapped him in Belgrade, took him to Slavonia. They killed him, covered him with cement, and threw him into the Danube. And a police inspector later came to tell me they couldn't do anything. Arkan was so dangerous that even the police couldn't do anything about him. So I had information about robberies. And only when I came here did I receive extensive documentation about the war crimes he was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you have any information about his activities with the Djeletovci oil expiration [sic]?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exploitation, you mean. I didn't hear of any explosion. I believe that, in many places where he went, he would kind of impose his presence so that he could go on doing whatever he pleased. I had information that for a while he appropriated this oil field, exported and sold that oil. The time of this story, of this text, is much closer to the time when it was all happening, and my memory now is certainly not so fresh as this text.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time are we -- let me check to see if we are able to display 65 ter number 2039.2?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could I have the next page in English, please. Thank you. And if I could have the next page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So what I'm interested in, Mr. Seselj, it's at the top of that page. And I will read the part in English that I -- I'm interested in. You're talking about Arkan, and at the end of that first full paragraph -- in the middle of the first full paragraph it begins: "In 1991, though, there was a war and what cannot be denied is that Arkan was a brave soldier in this war. His courage cannot be denied. He fought. He really fought. I can testify to this. But the problem is the other side of the coin. The problem lies in all the large-scale plundering that took place in the war and in which he was implicated. Then there's his link with the former president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Goran Hadzic ..." What link did you have in mind there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Hadzic and him?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or the authorities in Serbia? Well, I saw on more than one occasion that Arkan was appearing in various places together with Goran Hadzic, and based on that, I concluded there were ties between them. And then Arkan later imposed himself, thanks to Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and he'd simply do as he pleased. He went wherever he wanted to. He even attended sessions of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. He would come to the government session and nobody could do anything about it. Nobody even dared asked him --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- why he had come. As for ties with the regime in Serbia -- oh, you don't want me to say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I want you to slow down so I can catch up with the translation. I'd like to go back in time, back to 1990 when you were trying to have the Serbian Chetnik Movement registered. You talked about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, if I could please have 65 ter 6611, tab 137. And this is -- it was published in 1994 and it's dated 1990. And in the English, if we could go to the third page. In the English, could we have the next page, please, and the page after that. Sorry, the next page, obviously. Thank you. And in the B/C/S, if we could go to page 5, I think. Yes, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, this is the decision rejecting the application of the political party, the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Now, at the bottom of the page that you're looking at you can see the beginning of it, and when you're finished looking at that, I can move to the next page. Can I --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Move to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the same in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in the -- the statement of reasons, it's written here by the deputy, the republican secretary, that: "It is known from the recent history of Yugoslavia that members of the Chetnik movement in World War II ended the war on the losing side and their leaders were convicted as war criminals by people's courts because of massacres and other forms of terror against the peoples of Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Believing that the submitted name offends public morals in the Socialist Republic of Serbia, this secretariat has rejected the application of the political party, the Serbian Chetnik Movement ..." Is that what you meant yesterday by the Serbian Chetnik Movement being denied registration? Is this the document you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of 65 ter 6611.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could now move to tab 136, which is a one-page document. And it is 65 ter number 6610. I now fast-forward to 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now directing your attention to this, this, in fact, is a decision registering the Serbian Radical Party in 1991; correct? Is this the document you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it's -- for the record, it's dated 12 March 1991. And at this time we'd move for admission of 65 ter 110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And just to let the interpreters know, the next trio of clips that I'd like to play would be P88.50, and it would be the .3 document that you have, and the .8 document you have. And then Exhibit 2030. And then 65 ter 4936.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'd like to talk about Slobodan Milosevic and your relationship and the party's relationship with him. Now, in 1991, 1992, and 1993, you and your party were receiving assistance from him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We as a party never received any assistance from Milosevic. However, the Milosevic's regime helped us sending volunteers to Serbian Krajina. I told you how yesterday. Those volunteers had guaranteed labour rights, even privileges, in their workplaces. The federal authorities through the JNA provided additional guarantees. As I explained yesterday, Milosevic's regime tried as hard as they could to prevent successful mobilisation into the JNA. They feared that the generals would take an opportunity to topple himself and Tudjman. But he knew that he needed to help western Serbs. That's why his regime helped the sending of volunteers as of September 1991, when the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party started joining JNA units. Before September 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So in the future when I -- if I'm tapping my headphone it means that the interpretation needs to catch up to you. And if you could just stop, let the interpretation finish and then continue, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, I noticed your signals, but I misinterpreted them. I thought that they meant something entirely different. Now you have made the thing clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If the interpreters are ready, we can proceed with the playing of P88.50 and the first clip is -- will go from, I believe, 14:40 to 16:24. And the next clip will -- .8 will go from 37:41 to 38:48. May I get a confirmation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, if you please just listen and watch the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Therefore, we were in direct conflict with the regime and at that time Milosevic's policies were prominently Communist. His reversal came as late as 1991, when we -- some communication was established between us, meaning that he came over to our side instead of us coming over to his. "LS: And how did you ... when you signed up those volunteers for Knin, how did you obtain weapons, or how did they obtain them just in case they needed to do something there? "Seselj: We did not obtain weapons in 1990. We only signed up volunteers and sent them on occasion if there was a need to do so, but these were very small groups. In 1991 we began to organise greater numbers of volunteers and to send them to the front lines that had already been formed, particularly those in Eastern Slavonia and here in the eastern part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Our volunteers really proved themselves in the battle in Borovo Selo on 2nd May 1991, when they overpowered the more powerful Croatian forces, the Croatian police and parapolice forces. We received weapons from Milosevic's police, first from the then-minister of the interior, Radmilo Bogdanovic, and when he was replaced, from his successor. We also received old weapons from the Territorial Defence depots. These were old American Thompson rifles that had long been out of use, and old M-48 rifles, the so-called Tandzare. These were all obsolete and the army had stopped using them a long time ago, or had stored them in Territorial Defence depots. They didn't want to destroy them completely so they simply gave them to us. But it was these weapons that allowed us to defeat the Croats who were armed with modern weapons."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now moving to .8.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "LS: When you received those weapons, did that ... you said that the regime gave weapons to your party, I mean, the volunteers, was that in ... with the political leadership's, with Milosevic's knowledge, or through the police and through ... "Seselj: This was all done with Milosevic's knowledge, there's no doubt about that. And key people in the police with whom we co-operated at the time were Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mihajl Kertes and others ... Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki, who later commanded the Red Berets. From the General Staff, we mostly co-operated with General Domazetovic, who was the deputy chief of the General Staff and also at that time the head of the personnel administration, if I remember correctly. There were also contacts with lower-ranking officers and so on, depending on the need and the situation. Our volunteers came to Belgrade, the barracks in Bubanj Potok. That is where we put on uniforms, and where they were given weapons and buses to take them where they wanted. They were under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army as soon as the Yugoslav People's Army became involved in the fighting."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you interrupt the clip when it became the most interesting? It is like watching a western movie and somebody interrupts it at the moment of the showdown between the two opposing -- opponents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So it is true that Milosevic provided your volunteers with assistance in 1991, 1992, and 1993?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not as simple as that. There are two things that need be to clarified. When you say "Milosevic," he usually personified the regime itself. He was the most prominent politician in Serbia. His party was the ruling party without any competition. So when we say "Milosevic," we mean Milosevic's regime.
